title: Teleportation Game: Quantum Teleportation in Multi-Agent Systems for Interactive Music
authors: Eduardo Reck Miranda, Scott Yeiichi Oshiro
abstract: This paper introduces an interactive music system with quantum musical agents that communicate by teleporting quantum states to one another. Human performers interact in real time with agents whose melodic and rhythmic behaviours are encoded as quantum states using Single Qubit Probability Amplitude Modulation (SQPAM) and structured through Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE). Up to three agents are combined within a single quantum circuit, with directed communication via quantum teleportation. We are interested in supporting ambiguous, transformative interactions reminiscent of free Jazz improvisation. Therefore, rather than treating noise and decoherence as limitations, the system embraces NISQ-era constraints as creative affordances, framing agent communication as quantum whispers, that is, deliberate, musically expressive imperfections in state transfer. We provide demonstrations and analyses based on melodic correlation, pitch-set distance, and state fidelity, where a continuum between imitation and divergence can be observed. We developed a tunable interpretation method to assess how agents reinterpret teleported states. This work positions teleportation as a promising interaction mechanism for agent-based quantum computer music and outlines future directions toward distributed ensembles connected via the Quantum Internet.
summary: This work designs a novel interactive music system using quantum agents that communicate through quantum teleportation. It treats noise and decoherence not as failures, but as controllable parameters defining the 'interpretative distance' between musical ideas. This frames quantum communication in an artistic context, suggesting new ways to model complex, non-ideal interactions in quantum computation.
main_problem: To develop an interactive music system where quantum agents communicate via teleportation, supporting ambiguous interactions akin to free Jazz improvisation.
main_result: The paper demonstrates that agent interaction can be modeled as a continuous space of interpretative distance, rather than binary success/failure, by tuning the fidelity of state transfer.
method: It uses quantum teleportation protocols combined with Single Qubit Probability Amplitude Modulation (SQPAM) and Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) to encode musical features into quantum states.
model_or_system: The system operates on NISQ-era quantum computers, simulating multi-agent communication where the core mechanism is controlled unitary evolution ($U(	heta, \phi, \lambda)$) mediated by teleportation.
key_observables: Melodic correlation, pitch-set distance, state fidelity ($\mathcal{F}$), and Hamming Distance are used to quantify agent interaction quality.
important_parameters: The rotation angle $\theta$ in the interpreter module is crucial for tuning interpretative behavior; NISQ constraints themselves are treated as creative affordances ('quantum whispers').
main_assumptions: The system assumes that continuous audio features can be mapped effectively to discrete quantum gate parameters, and it embraces noise rather than treating it solely as an error.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall pipeline (Audio $\rightarrow$ Circuit $\rightarrow$ Teleportation $\rightarrow$ Output), single-agent circuits, multi-agent teleportation schemes, and fidelity distributions showing how varying parameters affects state overlap.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the full quantum agent system pipeline using feature extraction (Chunk 1) to implementing the core teleportation mechanism (Chunk 2), and finally refining the model by introducing a tunable interpreter module to analyze continuous interpretative behavior in multi-agent cascades (Chunks 3 & 4).
why_interesting: The focus on interpreting noise/decoherence as controllable, expressive parameters ($\theta$) provides an analogy for studying non-ideal quantum channels or open system dynamics where the 'error' itself carries information about the interaction.
